claim: Stu2/XMAP215 microtubule polymerases use multiple tubulin-binding TOG domains and a lattice-binding basic region to processively promote faster elongation.
source: Stu2/XMAP215 microtubule polymerases use multiple tubulin-binding TOG domains and a lattice-binding basic region to processively promote faster elongation.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known property of these polymerases, supported by prior research cited throughout the manuscript.

claim: Polymerase activity does not require different kinds of TOG domains.
source: We show that polymerase activity does not require different kinds of TOGs, nor are there strict requirements for how the TOGs are linked.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing that Stu2 variants with only TOG1 or only TOG2 domains retain polymerase activity.

claim: There are no strict requirements for how TOG domains are linked in the polymerase.
source: We show that polymerase activity does not require different kinds of TOGs, nor are there strict requirements for how the TOGs are linked.
evidence: This is supported by data showing that monomeric and dimeric variants with different TOG linkages can have comparable activity.

claim: An unexpected antagonism exists between the tubulin-binding TOGs and the lattice-binding basic region.
source: We identify an unexpected antagonism between the tubulin-binding TOGs and the lattice-binding basic region: lattice binding by the basic region is weak when at least two TOGs engage tubulins, strong when TOGs are empty.
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations showing differential lattice binding depending on TOG occupancy status.

claim: Lattice binding by the basic region is weak when at least two TOGs engage tubulins.
source: We identify an unexpected antagonism between the tubulin-binding TOGs and the lattice-binding basic region: lattice binding by the basic region is weak when at least two TOGs engage tubulins, strong when TOGs are empty.
evidence: This is demonstrated by TIRF microscopy experiments showing reduced lattice binding when TOGs are occupied.

claim: Lattice binding by the basic region is strong when TOGs are empty.
source: We identify an unexpected antagonism between the tubulin-binding TOGs and the lattice-binding basic region: lattice binding by the basic region is weak when at least two TOGs engage tubulins, strong when TOGs are empty.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experiments showing that 'doubly dead' Stu2 variants coat the microtubule lattice.

claim: End-localization of Stu2 requires unpolymerized tubulin.
source: End-localization of Stu2 requires unpolymerized tubulin, at least two TOGs, and polymerase competence.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing loss of end-localization in the absence of unpolymerized tubulin.

claim: End-localization of Stu2 requires at least two TOGs.
source: End-localization of Stu2 requires unpolymerized tubulin, at least two TOGs, and polymerase competence.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experiments showing that variants with only one active TOG do not show end-specific localization.

claim: End-localization of Stu2 requires polymerase competence.
source: End-localization of Stu2 requires unpolymerized tubulin, at least two TOGs, and polymerase competence.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that all conditions required for end-localization are also required for polymerase activity.

claim: Transfer of tubulin from TOGs to the lattice activates the basic region.
source: We propose a 'ratcheting' model for processivity: transfer of tubulin from TOGs to the lattice activates the basic region, retaining the polymerase at the end for subsequent rounds of tubulin binding and incorporation.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the observed antagonism between TOG:tubulin binding and basic:lattice interactions.

claim: Activation of the basic region retains the polymerase at the microtubule end for subsequent rounds of tubulin binding and incorporation.
source: We propose a 'ratcheting' model for processivity: transfer of tubulin from TOGs to the lattice activates the basic region, retaining the polymerase at the end for subsequent rounds of tubulin binding and incorporation.
evidence: This is part of the proposed ratcheting model to explain processivity based on experimental observations.

claim: Microtubules are dynamic polymers of αβ-tubulin.
source: Microtubules are dynamic polymers of αβ-tubulin (hereafter: tubulin) that have critical roles in chromosome segregation and intracellular organization (reviewed in Desai and Mitchison, 1997).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field, supported by citation to a review.

claim: Microtubules have critical roles in chromosome segregation and intracellular organization.
source: Microtubules are dynamic polymers of αβ-tubulin (hereafter: tubulin) that have critical roles in chromosome segregation and intracellular organization (reviewed in Desai and Mitchison, 1997).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to a review.

claim: Stu2/XMAP215 proteins regulate microtubule dynamics by making microtubules grow faster.
source: Evolutionarily conserved Stu2/XMAP215 proteins (Gard and Kirschner, 1987; Ohkura et al., 1988; Wang and Huffaker, 1997) regulate microtubule dynamics by making microtubules grow faster.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Fungal members of the Stu2/XMAP215 family like Stu2, Alp14, and Dis1 are homodimers.
source: Fungal members of this family like Stu2 (from S. cerevisiae) or Alp14 and Dis1 (from S. pombe) are homodimers, whereas orthologs in higher eukaryotes (e.g. Zyg-9 from C. elegans, XMAP215 from X. laevis, ch-TOG from H. sapiens, and others) are monomeric (Al-Bassam and Chang, 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Orthologs of Stu2/XMAP215 in higher eukaryotes are monomeric.
source: Fungal members of this family like Stu2 (from S. cerevisiae) or Alp14 and Dis1 (from S. pombe) are homodimers, whereas orthologs in higher eukaryotes (e.g. Zyg-9 from C. elegans, XMAP215 from X. laevis, ch-TOG from H. sapiens, and others) are monomeric (Al-Bassam and Chang, 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Stu2/XMAP215 proteins use multiple tubulin binding TOG domains to localize to the growing microtubule end and promote elongation.
source: Whether monomeric or dimeric, these essential proteins all use multiple tubulin binding tumor overexpressed gene (TOG) domains to localize to the growing microtubule end and promote elongation (Al-Bassam et al., 2012; 2006; Brouhard et al., 2008; Roostalu et al., 2015; Widlund et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: XMAP215 is a catalyst that increases the rate of microtubule elongation but not the apparent equilibrium.
source: Studies of XMAP215 (Brouhard et al., 2008) revealed that the polymerase (i) is a catalyst that increases the rate of microtubule elongation but not the apparent equilibrium, (ii) acts processively by performing multiple rounds of tubulin incorporation while on the growing end, and (iii) requires a minimum of two TOG domains.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work on XMAP215.

claim: XMAP215 acts processively by performing multiple rounds of tubulin incorporation while on the growing end.
source: Studies of XMAP215 (Brouhard et al., 2008) revealed that the polymerase (i) is a catalyst that increases the rate of microtubule elongation but not the apparent equilibrium, (ii) acts processively by performing multiple rounds of tubulin incorporation while on the growing end, and (iii) requires a minimum of two TOG domains.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work on XMAP215.

claim: XMAP215 requires a minimum of two TOG domains.
source: Studies of XMAP215 (Brouhard et al., 2008) revealed that the polymerase (i) is a catalyst that increases the rate of microtubule elongation but not the apparent equilibrium, (ii) acts processively by performing multiple rounds of tubulin incorporation while on the growing end, and (iii) requires a minimum of two TOG domains.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work on XMAP215.

claim: The basic region of Stu2/XMAP215 family polymerases is thought to provide lattice-binding affinity.
source: In addition to the TOGs, Stu2/XMAP215 family polymerases contain a basic region that is thought to provide lattice-binding affinity (Wang and Huffaker, 1997; Widlund et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: TOG1 and TOG2 domains from Stu2 each bind preferentially to curved tubulin.
source: Prior studies from our group revealed that the TOG1 and TOG2 domains from Stu2 each bind preferentially and with comparable affinity to curved tubulin (Ayaz et al., 2012, 2014), a conformation that is not compatible with the straight conformation of tubulin in the microtubule lattice.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work from the authors' group.

claim: TOG1 and TOG2 domains from Stu2 bind to curved tubulin with comparable affinity.
source: Prior studies from our group revealed that the TOG1 and TOG2 domains from Stu2 each bind preferentially and with comparable affinity to curved tubulin (Ayaz et al., 2012, 2014), a conformation that is not compatible with the straight conformation of tubulin in the microtubule lattice.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work from the authors' group.

claim: Curved tubulin is not compatible with the straight conformation of tubulin in the microtubule lattice.
source: Prior studies from our group revealed that the TOG1 and TOG2 domains from Stu2 each bind preferentially and with comparable affinity to curved tubulin (Ayaz et al., 2012, 2014), a conformation that is not compatible with the straight conformation of tubulin in the microtubule lattice.
evidence: This is established knowledge about tubulin conformations.

claim: Stu2 variants with either TOG1 or TOG2 inactivated were functional polymerases with maximal activity about half that of wild-type Stu2.
source: Stu2 variants with either TOG1 or TOG2 'inactivated' (mutated to essentially abolish interactions with tubulin, resulting in a molecule with only two functional TOG domains) were functional polymerases with maximal activity about half that of wild-type Stu2.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Stu2 coats the microtubule lattice without detectable end preference when its TOGs are 'empty'.
source: Stu2 coats the microtubule lattice without detectable end preference when its TOGs are 'empty', but this lattice binding is attenuated and plus-end specificity is restored when at least two TOGs engage unpolymerized tubulins.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Lattice binding by Stu2 is attenuated and plus-end specificity is restored when at least two TOGs engage unpolymerized tubulins.
source: Stu2 coats the microtubule lattice without detectable end preference when its TOGs are 'empty', but this lattice binding is attenuated and plus-end specificity is restored when at least two TOGs engage unpolymerized tubulins.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: Both polymerase activity and tubulin-induced attenuation of basic:lattice interactions were diminished by perturbations that make tubulin:tubulin interactions stronger.
source: Both polymerase activity and tubulin-induced attenuation of basic:lattice interactions were diminished by perturbations that make tubulin:tubulin interactions stronger.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data using β:T238A tubulin and Epothilone B shown in Figure 6.

claim: Perturbations that strengthen tubulin:tubulin interactions lead to futile cycling of the polymerase.
source: These perturbations apparently lead to futile cycling of the polymerase by bypassing the normal requirement for a microtubule end to stimulate release of TOG-bound tubulins.
evidence: This is an interpretation of experimental data showing loss of activity with stabilizing perturbations.

claim: The tubulin conformational cycle plays a central role in modulating the activity of Stu2/XMAP215 family polymerases.
source: Our findings provide new insights into how the design of the polymerase determines its activity, and reveal that the tubulin conformational cycle plays a more central role in modulating the activity of this family of polymerases than previously appreciated.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from experimental data showing effects of conformational perturbations.

claim: Stu2 forms a homodimer with each monomer containing TOG1, TOG2, a basic region, and a coiled-coil that mediates dimerization.
source: Stu2 forms a homodimer, with each monomer containing (from N to C) a TOG1 domain, a TOG2 domain, a basic region, and a coiled-coil that mediates dimerization (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: Stu2 variants track the growing ends of microtubules.
source: These assays revealed, consistent with prior work (Al-Bassam et al., 2006; Podolski et al., 2014), that Stu2 variants track the growing ends of microtubules (Figure 1B, right) and show dose-dependent stimulation of polymerization rates, reaching about 6-fold at saturation (Figure 1C; Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and citations to prior work.

claim: Stu2 shows dose-dependent stimulation of polymerization rates, reaching about 6-fold at saturation.
source: These assays revealed, consistent with prior work (Al-Bassam et al., 2006; Podolski et al., 2014), that Stu2 variants track the growing ends of microtubules (Figure 1B, right) and show dose-dependent stimulation of polymerization rates, reaching about 6-fold at saturation (Figure 1C; Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Stu2(TOG1*-TOG2) yielded approximately 40% maximal fold-stimulation of elongation compared to wild-type.
source: Stu2(TOG1*-TOG2) yielded ~40% maximal fold-stimulation of elongation compared to wild-type (Figure 1C,F); Stu2(TOG1-TOG2*) yielded ~60% (Figure 1C,F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C and 1F.

claim: Stu2(TOG1-TOG2*) yielded approximately 60% maximal fold-stimulation of elongation compared to wild-type.
source: Stu2(TOG1*-TOG2) yielded ~40% maximal fold-stimulation of elongation compared to wild-type (Figure 1C,F); Stu2(TOG1-TOG2*) yielded ~60% (Figure 1C,F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C and 1F.

claim: Both Stu2(TOG1*-TOG2) and Stu2(TOG1-TOG2*) retained high-affinity end-binding.
source: Both variants retained high-affinity end-binding (Figure 1F), as evidenced by the hyperbolic activity vs concentration behavior.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Stu2(TOG2-TOG2) yielded a polymerase that is only slightly weaker than wild-type with 5.1-fold maximal stimulation compared to 6.1-fold for wild-type.
source: Consistent with this idea, substituting TOG1 with a second copy of TOG2 (denoted Stu2(TOG2-TOG2)) yielded a polymerase that is only slightly weaker than wild-type (5.1-fold maximal stimulation for TOG2-TOG2 compared to 6.1-fold for wild-type) (Figure 1E,F, see also Figure 1—figure supplement 1; Figure 1—figure supplement 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E and 1F.

claim: Stu2(TOG1-TOG1) yielded an active polymerase, although less active than TOG2-TOG2.
source: Substituting TOG2 with a second copy of TOG1 (denoted Stu2(TOG1-TOG1)) also yielded an active polymerase, although less so than for TOG2-TOG2 (Figure 1E,F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E and 1F.

claim: Reducing the number of active TOGs from 4 to 2 reduced polymerase activity approximately 2-fold without weakening end-association.
source: In summary, different kinds of tubulin-binding TOG domains are not required to support activity, and reducing the number of 'active' TOGs from 4 to 2 reduced polymerase activity approximately 2-fold without weakening end-association.
evidence: This is a summary of experimental data from Figure 1.

claim: Monomeric Stu2-∆cc displayed a substantial decrease in activity as well as greatly reduced end-binding affinity compared to dimeric variants.
source: Stu2-∆cc displayed a substantial decrease in activity as well as greatly reduced end-binding affinity compared to dimeric variants (Figure 1D,F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D and 1F.

claim: Supercharging the basic region of monomeric Stu2-∆cc-2xBasic restored high-affinity end-binding.
source: 'Supercharging' the basic region restored high-affinity end-binding (Figure 1D,F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D and 1F.

claim: The supercharged monomeric polymerase showed maximal fold-stimulation of elongation rates comparable to dimeric Stu2(TOG1*-TOG2) or Stu2(TOG1-TOG2*) polymerases.
source: The supercharged monomeric polymerase also showed maximal fold-stimulation of elongation rates comparable to the dimeric Stu2(TOG1*-TOG2) or Stu2(TOG1-TOG2*) polymerases that also operate with only two active TOGs (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Polymerase activity of Stu2 is approximately proportional to the number of tubulin-binding TOG domains when positioned as in wild-type.
source: The experiments described in this section demonstrate that the polymerase activity of Stu2: (i) does not strictly require different kinds of TOG, (ii) is approximately proportional to the number of tubulin-binding TOG domains (when positioned as in wild-type), and (iii) is modulated by the 'strength' of the basic region (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from experimental data presented in Figure 1.

claim: Polymerase activity of Stu2 is modulated by the strength of the basic region.
source: The experiments described in this section demonstrate that the polymerase activity of Stu2: (i) does not strictly require different kinds of TOG, (ii) is approximately proportional to the number of tubulin-binding TOG domains (when positioned as in wild-type), and (iii) is modulated by the 'strength' of the basic region (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing effects of basic region charge on activity.

claim: Monomeric and dimeric two-TOG polymerases show comparable activity as long as their respective basic regions have similar charge.
source: The observation that monomeric and dimeric 'two TOG' polymerases show comparable activity as long as their respective basic regions have similar charge indicates that how the active TOGs are linked is of little importance for polymerase activity.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from experimental data comparing monomeric and dimeric variants.

claim: How the active TOGs are linked is of little importance for polymerase activity.
source: The observation that monomeric and dimeric 'two TOG' polymerases show comparable activity as long as their respective basic regions have similar charge indicates that how the active TOGs are linked is of little importance for polymerase activity.
evidence: This is inferred from experimental data showing comparable activity despite different linkages.

claim: Dimeric polymerases like Stu2/Alp14 and monomeric polymerases like XMAP215/chTOG share a common mechanism.
source: Such loose requirements on the elements linking the TOGs suggests that dimeric polymerases like Stu2/Alp14 and monomeric polymerases like XMAP215/chTOG share a common mechanism despite having different oligomerization states.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that oligomerization state does not strongly affect activity.

claim: The concentration-dependence of end-binding for Stu2 is comparable to the concentration-dependence for activity.
source: A hyperbolic fit to the concentration-dependent fluorescence yielded a concentration at half-maximal intensity of 20 nM. The concentration-dependence of end-binding for Stu2 is comparable to the concentration-dependence we observed for activity (60 nM, see Figure 1F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from fluorescence intensity measurements.

claim: The microtubule end can support approximately one Stu2 dimer for every two protofilaments.
source: If we assume (supported by photobleaching analysis, see next section) that the intensity measurements at 5 nM Stu2 reflect individual Stu2 dimers on the microtubule end, then the saturating fluorescence corresponds to ~6 Stu2 dimers on the microtubule end. Thus, the microtubule end can support approximately one Stu2 dimer for every two protofilaments.
evidence: This is calculated from fluorescence intensity measurements and photobleaching analysis.

claim: Stu2(TOG1*-TOG2) was present on the microtubule end in amounts comparable to wild-type.
source: Whereas Stu2(TOG1*-TOG2) was present in amounts comparable to wild-type, Stu2(TOG1-TOG2*) only reached about half that level (Figure 2B; Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Stu2(TOG1-TOG2*) only reached about half the end accumulation level of wild-type.
source: Whereas Stu2(TOG1*-TOG2) was present in amounts comparable to wild-type, Stu2(TOG1-TOG2*) only reached about half that level (Figure 2B; Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Stu2(TOG2-TOG2*) accumulated to comparable levels as TOG1-TOG2*.
source: Stu2(TOG2-TOG2*) (wherein the natural TOG1 domain was replaced with a TOG2) accumulated to comparable levels as TOG1-TOG2* (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: A positional effect contributes to specify the degree of end accumulation of Stu2.
source: Thus, installing a TOG2 domain in the N-terminal position where TOG1 normally resides did not compensate for the inactivation of TOG2 in its natural position. This provides clear evidence that a positional effect – for example proximity to the basic region - contributes to specify the degree of end accumulation.
evidence: This is inferred from experimental data showing that TOG identity alone does not determine accumulation.

claim: Stu2(TOG1-TOG2*) shows 20% higher specific activity than wild-type Stu2.
source: Indeed, after normalizing by the different saturating amounts of polymerase on the microtubule end, Stu2(TOG1-TOG2*) shows 20% higher specific activity than wild-type Stu2 (Figure 2C), despite having half as many active (non-mutated) TOGs.
evidence: This is calculated from experimental data after normalizing for end accumulation.

claim: On a per-active-TOG basis, the specific activity of Stu2(TOG1-TOG2*) is over two-fold higher than wild-type.
source: On a per-active-TOG basis, the specific activity of Stu2(TOG1-TOG2*) is over two-fold higher than wild-type (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is calculated from experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Deleting TOG2 completely abolished polymerase activity and end association/tracking.
source: However, deleting the TOG2 domain completely abolished polymerase activity and end association/tracking (Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The lack of activity in TOG2-deleted variants reflects the positioning of the active TOG domain relative to the basic region, not the nature of the active TOG.
source: This dramatic loss of function could not be rescued by installing a TOG2 domain in place of TOG1 (Figure 2D), so the lack of activity must reflect the positioning of the active TOG domain relative to the basic region, not the nature of the active TOG.
evidence: This is inferred from experimental data showing that TOG identity cannot rescue the deletion.

claim: Proximity of a TOG domain to the basic region is important for polymerase activity.
source: These data, together with the data from Stu2(TOG1-TOG1) that also introduced extra sequence between the basic region and the preceding TOG (Figure 1E), indicate that proximity of a TOG domain to the basic region is important.
evidence: This is inferred from experimental data showing effects of spacing on activity.

claim: Deleting TOG2 compromised genetic rescue most severely whereas mutating TOG2, or deleting or mutating TOG1, affected rescue less severely.
source: A genetic rescue assay provides additional support for the special nature of the basic-proximal TOG2 domain: deleting TOG2 compromised rescue most severely whereas mutating TOG2, or deleting or mutating TOG1 domain, affected rescue less severely (and comparably to each other) (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by genetic rescue assay data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Stu2 function does not have an absolute requirement for a TOG2 domain next to the basic region.
source: Stu2 function does not appear to have an absolute requirement for a TOG2 domain next to the basic region, because Stu2(TOG1-TOG1), a construct entirely lacking TOG2 domains, showed appreciable rescue activity (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C; slightly different domain boundaries for the transplanted TOG1 were used in the rescue constructs compared to the in vitro experiments described above, see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is supported by genetic rescue data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: There is a special requirement for a basic-proximal TOG domain.
source: We conclude that there is a special requirement for a basic-proximal TOG domain, and that there might be some separation of function between TOG1 and TOG2 at this position.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple experimental observations.

claim: When the concentration of Stu2 is 5 nM, there should be on average 1.2 Stu2 dimers on the microtubule end.
source: The hyperbolic fit to the fluorescence intensity of Stu2 on the microtubule end indicates that when the concentration of Stu2 is 5 nM (1/4 of the apparent dissociation constant for tip binding, see Figure 2A), there should be on average 1.2 Stu2 dimers on the microtubule end.
evidence: This is calculated from the hyperbolic fit to fluorescence intensity data.

claim: The characteristic residence time of Stu2 at low concentration (5 nM) is 2.2 seconds.
source: We fit a one-phase exponential decay to the histogram of end residence times, which yielded a characteristic residence time of 2.2 s (Figure 3B, black, 3D; Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B and 3D.

claim: The characteristic residence time of Stu2 at high concentration (200 nM) is 1.98 seconds.
source: We performed 'spike' experiments (5 nM Stu2-GFP + 195 nM unlabeled Stu2) to monitor the behavior of individual Stu2 polymerases under conditions where Stu2 was substantially increasing growth rates. We observed short fluorescent Stu2 'tracks' in these 'spike' experiments, and the distribution of dwell times yielded a characteristic residence time of 1.98 s (Figure 3B, orange, 3D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B and 3D.

claim: The characteristic residence times for Stu2 at high and low concentrations are quite similar.
source: The characteristic residence times for Stu2 at high and low concentrations are quite similar, and are also the same order of magnitude as that measured for XMAP215 (3.8 s).
evidence: This is a comparison of experimental measurements.

claim: Each Stu2 polymerase adds approximately 16 tubulins during its residence time.
source: 200 nM Stu2 increases the microtubule elongation rate ~1.8 μm/min over the control (equivalent to 49 tubulins per second), and at this concentration we estimate that there are ~6 Stu2 polymerases on the end. If 6 Stu2s on average account for ~98 tubulins in 2 s (the measured residence time), then each Stu2 adds ~16 tubulins.
evidence: This is calculated from experimental measurements of growth rates and residence times.

claim: Stu2 is a modestly processive polymerase.
source: Thus, like XMAP215, Stu2 is a modestly processive polymerase.
evidence: This is concluded from processivity measurements showing ~16 tubulins added per polymerase.

claim: Inactivating the TOG1 domain yielded a modest decrease in dwell times to 1.7 seconds for Stu2(TOG1*-TOG2) compared to 2.2 seconds for wild-type.
source: Inactivating the TOG1 domain yielded a modest decrease in dwell times (1.7 s for Stu2(TOG1*-TOG2) compared to 2.2 s for wild-type) (Figure 3C,D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C and 3D.

claim: Inactivating the TOG2 domain almost doubled the polymerase dwell time to 4.0 seconds for Stu2(TOG1-TOG2*).
source: In contrast, inactivating the TOG2 domain almost doubled the polymerase dwell time (to 4.0 s for Stu2(TOG1-TOG2*)) (Figure 3C,D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C and 3D.

claim: Stu2(TOG2-TOG2*) showed a nearly two-fold increase in end-residence time to 3.9 seconds compared to 2.2 seconds for wild-type.
source: This enhanced end residence of Stu2(TOG1-TOG2*) could not be ascribed to some TOG1-specific property, because Stu2(TOG2-TOG2*) also showed a nearly two-fold increase in end-residence time (3.9 s for Stu2(TOG2-TOG2*) compared to 2.2 s for wild-type) (Figure 3C,D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C and 3D.

claim: Inactivating tubulin binding by the basic-proximal TOG domain increases dwell time and presumably processivity.
source: Thus, inactivating tubulin binding by the basic-proximal TOG domain actually increases dwell time (and presumably processivity); deleting the TOG2 domain (Stu2(TOG1-∆TOG2)) abolished end tracking entirely.
evidence: This is concluded from experimental data showing increased residence times with TOG2 inactivation.

claim: Current models for XMAP215/Stu2 family polymerases assume that lattice binding by the basic domain is independent of tubulin binding by the TOGs.
source: Current models for XMAP215/Stu2 family polymerases assume that lattice binding by the basic domain is independent of tubulin binding by the TOGs (e.g [Ayaz et al., 2014; Widlund et al., 2011]).
evidence: This is stated as a description of existing models with citations.

claim: The doubly dead Stu2(TOG1*-TOG2*) variant failed to stimulate growth rate.
source: As expected, the doubly dead variant failed to stimulate growth rate (Figure 4—figure supplement 1; Figure 4—figure supplement 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The doubly dead Stu2(TOG1*-TOG2*) variant robustly coated the lattice without detectable end preference.
source: Unexpectedly, the doubly dead variant robustly coated the lattice, without detectable end preference (Figure 4).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Interactions between TOGs and unpolymerized tubulin attenuate lattice binding by the basic region of Stu2.
source: These results indicate that interactions between TOGs and unpolymerized tubulin attenuate lattice binding by the basic region of Stu2.
evidence: This is concluded from experimental observations of differential lattice binding.

claim: Dimeric polymerases with TOG1 or TOG2 inactivated showed robust tip localization with little binding to the bulk lattice.
source: Dimeric polymerases with TOG1 or TOG2 inactivated (Stu2(TOG1*-TOG2) or Stu2(TOG1-TOG2*)) showed robust tip localization with little binding to the bulk lattice (Figure 4).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Monomeric Stu2-∆cc-2xBasic with one TOG inactivated showed strong binding to the lattice without detectable tip preference.
source: However, when one of the two TOGs in this monomeric construct was mutated (e.g. Stu2(TOG1*-TOG2)∆cc-2xBasic), we observed strong binding to the lattice without detectable tip preference (Figure 4); polymerase activity was also lost (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: At least two TOG:tubulin interactions are required to attenuate the lattice binding activity of Stu2.
source: Thus, at least two TOG:tubulin interactions are required to attenuate the lattice binding activity of Stu2.
evidence: This is concluded from experimental data showing lattice binding with fewer than two active TOGs.

claim: Stu2 coated the lattice of stabilized microtubules when there was no unpolymerized tubulin present in the assay.
source: Control experiments recapitulated the effects we observed on dynamic microtubules: Stu2 coated the lattice of stabilized microtubules when there was no unpolymerized tubulin present in the assay, and this lattice coating was lost with the addition of unpolymerized wild-type tubulin (Figure 5B, left).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Lattice coating by Stu2 was lost with the addition of unpolymerized wild-type tubulin.
source: Control experiments recapitulated the effects we observed on dynamic microtubules: Stu2 coated the lattice of stabilized microtubules when there was no unpolymerized tubulin present in the assay, and this lattice coating was lost with the addition of unpolymerized wild-type tubulin (Figure 5B, left).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Tail-less tubulin lacking the C-terminii of α- and β-tubulin inhibited Stu2 binding to the lattice.
source: We first speculated that the negatively charged C-terminii of TOG-bound tubulins might themselves bind to the basic region, effectively competing with the microtubule lattice for the basic region. To test this idea, we purified 'tail-less' tubulin lacking the C-terminii of α- and β-tubulin. This tail-less tubulin also inhibited Stu2 binding to the lattice (Figure 5B, middle panel).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Competing interactions between the basic region and the charged C-terminii of TOG-bound tubulins cannot explain the tubulin-induced attenuation of lattice binding.
source: Thus, competing interactions between the basic region and the charged C-terminii of the TOG-bound tubulins cannot explain the tubulin-induced attenuation of lattice binding.
evidence: This is concluded from experimental data showing that tail-less tubulin still attenuates lattice binding.

claim: Longitudinal interactions between TOG-bound tubulins do not appear to be important for the tubulin-induced attenuation of lattice binding.
source: Longitudinal interactions between the TOG-bound tubulins do not appear to be important for the tubulin-induced attenuation of lattice binding, because tubulin 'blocked' on its minus-end (T350E α-tubulin; [Johnson et al., 2011], Figure 5B) or on its plus-end (T175R, V179R β-tubulin; [Johnson et al., 2011], Figure 5—figure supplement 2) attenuated lattice binding by Stu2 comparably to wild-type tubulin.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Lateral contacts between TOG-bound tubulins are important for the tubulin-induced antagonism of basic:lattice interactions.
source: By contrast, Stu2 remained bound to the lattice in the presence of tubulin carrying mutations at the site of lateral interactions between heterodimers (Alushin et al., 2014)(H284A on α-tubulin, Figure 5—figure supplement 2; or F281A on β-tubulin, Figure 5B, left) Thus, lateral contacts between TOG-bound tubulins are important for the tubulin-induced antagonism of basic:lattice interactions.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: For Stu2, there is antagonistic coupling between TOG:tubulin and basic:lattice interactions.
source: The data described in this section reveal that for Stu2, there is antagonistic coupling between TOG:tubulin and basic:lattice interactions: when at least two TOGs on a given polymerase each engage a tubulin, lateral interactions (possibly transient) between those TOG-bound tubulins substantially reduce lattice-binding affinity (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from experimental data on tubulin mutants.

claim: Zyg-9 coated microtubules in the absence of unpolymerized tubulin.
source: Like Stu2, Zyg-9 coated microtubules in the absence of unpolymerized tubulin, and lattice binding by Zyg-9 was greatly attenuated in the presence of unpolymerized tubulin (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Lattice binding by Zyg-9 was greatly attenuated in the presence of unpolymerized tubulin.
source: Like Stu2, Zyg-9 coated microtubules in the absence of unpolymerized tubulin, and lattice binding by Zyg-9 was greatly attenuated in the presence of unpolymerized tubulin (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Reciprocal antagonism between lattice binding and TOGs engaging unpolymerized tubulin is a conserved feature of the Stu2/XMAP215 family of polymerases.
source: Thus, it appears that reciprocal antagonism between lattice binding and TOGs engaging unpolymerized tubulin is a conserved feature of the Stu2/XMAP215 family of polymerases.
evidence: This is concluded from experimental data showing similar behavior in Stu2 and Zyg-9.

claim: Tub2:T238A tubulin retains a curved conformation in the unpolymerized state.
source: We previously characterized a tubulin 'conformation cycle' mutant, Tub2:T238A (henceforth β:T238A) (Geyer et al., 2015). This mutant retains a curved conformation in the unpolymerized state, but it stabilizes microtubules by adopting a more GTP-like conformation in the GDP lattice.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work from the authors' group.

claim: Tub2:T238A tubulin stabilizes microtubules by adopting a more GTP-like conformation in the GDP lattice.
source: We previously characterized a tubulin 'conformation cycle' mutant, Tub2:T238A (henceforth β:T238A) (Geyer et al., 2015). This mutant retains a curved conformation in the unpolymerized state, but it stabilizes microtubules by adopting a more GTP-like conformation in the GDP lattice.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work from the authors' group.

claim: The effects of Tub2:T238A are reminiscent of how taxol allosterically stabilizes microtubules.
source: These effects are reminiscent of how the small molecule taxol allosterically stabilizes microtubules (Alushin et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a comparison to known effects of taxol, supported by citation.

claim: Stu2 barely stimulated elongation and showed weak to no plus-end specificity on dynamic β:T238A microtubules.
source: To our surprise, Stu2 barely stimulated elongation and showed weak to no plus-end specificity on dynamic β:T238A microtubules (Figure 6A,B; Figure 6—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A and 6B.

claim: Stu2 coated the lattice of β:T238A microtubules.
source: Instead, Stu2 coated the lattice of these mutant microtubules, reminiscent of what we observed for the 'doubly dead' polymerase Stu2(TOG1*-TOG2*), the TOGs of which are inactivated for tubulin binding.
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The β:T238A mutation does not cause a defect in the interactions between individual TOGs and tubulin.
source: In this case, however, the mutation in β-tubulin does not cause a defect in the interactions between individual TOGs and β:T238A tubulin: isolated TOG1 or TOG2 domains bind to wild-type and to β:T238A tubulin with comparable affinity (Geyer et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work from the authors' group.

claim: End-tracking is lost and lattice binding is enhanced when wild-type tubulin is used with the microtubule-stabilizing drug Epothilone-B.
source: Polymerase assays using wild-type yeast tubulin with a low concentration (4 μM) of Epothilone B yielded results very similar to those obtained with β:T238A tubulin: Stu2 coated the lattice, and polymerase activity and plus-end tracking were greatly reduced (Figure 6A,B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A and 6B.

claim: Two independent perturbations that promote tubulin:tubulin interactions increase lattice binding by Stu2 while decreasing its polymerase activity.
source: Thus, two independent perturbations that promote tubulin:tubulin interactions increase lattice binding by Stu2 while decreasing its polymerase activity.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from experimental data with β:T238A tubulin and Epothilone B.

claim: Normal polymerase function requires that TOG-bound tubulins resist self-association-induced straightening enough to ensure that their release from the polymerase occurs only at the microtubule end.
source: We infer that normal polymerase function requires not only that the TOG-bound tubulins be curved, but also that they resist self-association-induced straightening enough to ensure that their release from the polymerase occurs only at the microtubule end (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is inferred from experimental data showing loss of activity with stabilizing perturbations.

claim: Polymerase activity does not depend strongly on oligomerization state.
source: Monomeric Stu2 variants with a 'dimer equivalent' basic domain stimulate elongation to a comparable extent as homodimeric variants with an equal number of tubulin-binding TOG domains, so polymerase activity also does not depend strongly on oligomerization state.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from experimental data comparing monomeric and dimeric variants.

claim: Polymerase activity is largely insensitive to the way that the TOGs are linked.
source: That monomeric and dimeric Stu2 variants can have comparable activity indicates that polymerase activity is largely insensitive to the way that the TOGs are linked.
evidence: This is inferred from experimental data showing comparable activity with different linkages.

claim: The presence of two functional TOG domains was not always sufficient for full polymerase activity.
source: In an earlier study, we found that Stu2 variants with either TOG1 or TOG2 inactivated for tubulin-binding rescued the loss of wild-type Stu2 in a genetic assay, but monomeric forms of Stu2 showed much poorer rescue activity (Ayaz et al., 2014). These results suggested that the presence of two functional TOG domains was not always sufficient for full polymerase activity, and consequently that dimerization and/or how the TOGs were linked was essential for function.
evidence: This is stated as a prior finding from the authors' earlier work, supported by citation.

claim: Deletion of the TOG2 domain eliminated plus-end selective localization in addition to abolishing polymerase activity.
source: Deletion of the TOG2 domain eliminated plus-end selective localization (Figure 2D) in addition to abolishing polymerase activity (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Plus-end specific localization requires at least two active TOGs and interactions with unpolymerized tubulin.
source: Thus, plus-end specific localization requires at least two active TOGs and interactions with unpolymerized tubulin, the same requirements for polymerase activity.
evidence: This is concluded from experimental observations of variants lacking these features.

claim: Plus-end specific localization depends on polymerase activity.
source: The simplest explanation for these shared minimal requirements is that plus-end specific localization actually depends on polymerase activity.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that requirements for localization and activity are the same.

claim: A synthetic polymerase can be constructed from TOG1-TOG2 and an unrelated basic element.
source: A synthetic polymerase can be constructed from TOG1-TOG2 and an unrelated basic element (Widlund et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Polymerases carrying tubulins must be specifically disadvantaged for diffusing on the lattice compared to empty polymerases.
source: Thus, compared to empty polymerases, polymerases carrying tubulins must be specifically disadvantaged for diffusing on the lattice.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that lattice binding is attenuated when TOGs are occupied.

claim: Polymerases diffusing to the microtubule end will for the most part arrive empty.
source: This in turn means that polymerases diffusing to the microtubule end will for the most part arrive 'empty'.
evidence: This is inferred from the disadvantage of tubulin-loaded polymerases for lattice diffusion.

claim: Diffusive tubulin shuttling to the end will make little contribution to polymerase activity.
source: Consequently, diffusive 'tubulin shuttling' to the end will make little contribution to polymerase activity.
evidence: This is inferred from the conclusion that polymerases arrive at the end empty.

claim: Diminishing the energetic cost of self-association-induced tubulin straightening leads to nonproductive release of polymerase-bound tubulins away from the microtubule end.
source: By contrast, in the presence of mutation- or drug-induced perturbations that strengthen tubulin self-association and straightening, Stu2 behaves as if it were empty: it binds the lattice without detectable end preference. Thus, diminishing the energetic cost of self-association-induced tubulin straightening must lead to nonproductive release of polymerase-bound tubulins away from the microtubule end.
evidence: This is inferred from experimental observations with stabilizing perturbations.

claim: Nonproductive release of tubulins eliminates preferential end binding by Stu2.
source: That this nonproductive release also eliminates preferential end binding by Stu2 reveals an unanticipated link between polymerase mechanism and the tubulin conformation cycle.
evidence: This is concluded from experimental observations showing loss of end preference with stabilizing perturbations.

claim: If tubulin straightens too easily, polymerase activity is lost to futile cycling.
source: If tubulin straightens too easily, polymerase activity is lost to futile cycling, in which straightening-induced release from TOGs is no longer restricted to the microtubule end.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism to explain experimental observations with stabilizing perturbations.

claim: The comparison of Stu2/XMAP215 family polymerases to formins is no longer apt.
source: Stu2/XMAP215 family polymerases have been compared to formins (Brouhard et al., 2008), which are unrelated polymerases that promote fast elongation of actin filaments (reviewed in [Goode and Eck, 2007]). This comparison no longer seems apt.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the findings of this study compared to known properties of formins.

claim: For formins, end localization can be separated from polymerase activity.
source: For the highly processive formins, end localization can be separated from polymerase activity (Li and Higgs, 2003; Pruyne et al., 2002; Kovar et al., 2006; Otomo et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work on formins.

claim: In modestly processive Stu2, end localization and polymerase activity appear to be inseparable.
source: However, in modestly processive Stu2, end localization and polymerase activity appear to be inseparable.
evidence: This is concluded from experimental observations showing shared requirements.

claim: Ena/VASP proteins enhance actin elongation through a tethering mechanism.
source: Indeed, Ena/VASP proteins enhance actin elongation through a tethering mechanism (Breitsprecher et al., 2011; Hansen and Mullins, 2010; Winkelman et al., 2014) that uses WH2-like domains, some of which operate analogously to TOGs because they bind preferentially to unpolymerized (actin) subunits (Bachmann et al., 1999; Hüttelmaier et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work on Ena/VASP.

claim: Ena/VASP proteins are only weakly processive.
source: Ena/VASP proteins share three other functional characteristics with Stu2 that formins do not: (i) Ena/VASP proteins are only weakly processive, (ii) their polymer 'side binding' is attenuated in the presence of unpolymerized monomers, and (iii) their end localization requires interactions with unpolymerized monomers (Hansen and Mullins, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work on Ena/VASP.

claim: Ena/VASP polymer side binding is attenuated in the presence of unpolymerized monomers.
source: Ena/VASP proteins share three other functional characteristics with Stu2 that formins do not: (i) Ena/VASP proteins are only weakly processive, (ii) their polymer 'side binding' is attenuated in the presence of unpolymerized monomers, and (iii) their end localization requires interactions with unpolymerized monomers (Hansen and Mullins, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work on Ena/VASP.

claim: Ena/VASP end localization requires interactions with unpolymerized monomers.
source: Ena/VASP proteins share three other functional characteristics with Stu2 that formins do not: (i) Ena/VASP proteins are only weakly processive, (ii) their polymer 'side binding' is attenuated in the presence of unpolymerized monomers, and (iii) their end localization requires interactions with unpolymerized monomers (Hansen and Mullins, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work on Ena/VASP.

claim: For both Stu2 and Ena/VASP, processivity emerges from the ability of the polymerase to alternate between stronger and weaker states of lattice association controlled by whether unpolymerized subunits are bound.
source: For both Stu2 and for Ena/VASP, it seems that processivity emerges from the ability of the polymerase to alternate between stronger and weaker states of lattice association in a way that is controlled by whether or not unpolymerized subunits are bound (Figure 7; see also [Hansen and Mullins, 2010; Breitsprecher et al., 2011]).
evidence: This is a proposed model based on experimental observations and comparison to Ena/VASP.

claim: Ratcheting by alternating engagement between TOGs and the basic region is a design principle of the polymerase that provides a model to explain its processive action.
source: While for Stu2 it is clear that tethering-based transfer of monomers from TOGs to the polymer end can promote faster elongation, some other post-delivery mechanism is required to maintain the polymerase at the microtubule end for subsequent rounds of delivery. Ratcheting by alternating engagement between TOGs and the basic region is a design principle of the polymerase that provides a simple conceptual model to explain its processive action.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on experimental findings.
